extracted.intended_audience: stand-up comedians, joke writers, and performers working with personal/vulnerability material
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing and performing personal stand-up that leans on character voices and intimate vulnerability; emphasizes specificity, ethical distance, and testing material in small rooms. Useful for comedians crafting bits about mental illness, family, and other sensitive subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice work as the joke engine
rubrics_metrics.description: Bamford's signature is voice characters embedded in narrative bits; the character voice DELIVERS the joke while the comic acts as narrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use character voices to carry punchlines; position yourself as the narrator so the character can speak truths or say things you cannot. This creates ethical distance that allows you to voice otherwise unsayable lines. Preference for embedded character bits over straightforward one-person delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character can say things the comic cannot (ethical distance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The character can say things the comic cannot — the voice creates ethical distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the character's separateness to try riskier or transgressive lines without exposing the performer personally; the distance permits content that would feel exploitative or dangerous if stated directly by the comedian.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity transforms confessional into comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The bit is not 'look at how broken I am.' The bit is 'here is the absurd specific texture of how broken I am.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make vulnerability specific and textured rather than vague. Concrete, absurd specifics make confessional material funny and relatable; vague statements remain confessional and solicit pity rather than laughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid asking for pity; invite recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Bamford never asks the audience to pity her; she invites them to recognize themselves in her specifics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame vulnerable material so audiences see themselves in the detail; ensure the laugh arises from recognition and shared humanity rather than superiority or pity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family material: impersonate, don't describe
rubrics_metrics.description: The family is impersonated, not described. The voice impressions confer love; the audience hears the affection in the mimicry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use affectionate impersonations to humanize family members; impersonation (with warmth) lets hard family material land warmly rather than as attack or complaint. Avoid flat descriptions; show through voice and behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small-room honesty and discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Bamford has performed entire shows for one person. The small room is honest in ways the big room isn't.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work material in very small, intimate settings to reveal what truly lands. The discipline of performing for small audiences tightens joke writing and exposure choices. Test whether the bit still works for a single audience member.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survivability: does the joke hold for one person?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the joke survive an audience of one?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 'audience of one' as a litmus test: if a joke still elicits recognition/laughter in the smallest setting, it's likely robust. If it relies on crowd dynamics, consider reworking for specificity or voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ethical distance to say the unsayable
rubrics_metrics.description: Are you using ethical distance to say the unsayable?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the device (character, impersonation, narratorial framing) sufficiently shields you so the content reads as comedic exploration rather than personal confession or exploitation. If not, reframe or increase specificity/affection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Could a character deliver the line better than you?
rubrics_metrics.description: Could a CHARACTER deliver the line better than you?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether shifting the line to a distinct voice/character improves its comedic effect. If yes, rewrite into character voice; if no, keep it in narrator voice or rework the line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the voice impression carrying affection?
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the voice impression carrying affection?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm that impressions of others—family members or characters—communicate warmth rather than mockery. Affection in impressionality protects relationships and helps audiences empathize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have you made vulnerability specific, not vague?
rubrics_metrics.description: Have you made vulnerability specific, not vague?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete details, odd observations, and absurd textures convert vulnerability into comedic material. Replace general statements of brokenness with sharp, singular images or behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Are you inviting recognition, not pity?
rubrics_metrics.description: Are you inviting recognition, not pity?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame bits so audiences recognize shared feelings or situations. Avoid cues that solicit sympathy; instead aim for universality through specificity so laughter comes from connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the joke survive an audience of one?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the joke survive an audience of one?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Duplicate deliberate check from working rubric) Use the smallest possible audience as a test of joke strength. If a joke fails in extreme intimacy, it likely depends on external factors rather than intrinsic comedic truth.
